description_full: AutoNation, Inc., through its subsidiaries, operates as an automotive retailer in the United States. The company operates through four segments: Domestic, Import, Premium Luxury, and AutoNation Finance. It offers a range of automotive products and services, including new and used vehicles; and parts and services, such as automotive repair and maintenance, and wholesale parts and collision services. The company also provides automotive finance and insurance products comprising vehicle services and other protection products; and indirect financing, as well as arranges finance for vehicle purchases through third-party finance sources. It owns and operates new vehicle franchises from stores located in metropolitan markets in the Sunbelt region, as well as AutoNation-branded collision centers, AutoNation USA used vehicle stores, AutoNation-branded automotive auction operations, and parts distribution centers. The company was formerly known as Republic Industries, Inc. and changed its name to AutoNation, Inc. in 1999. AutoNation, Inc. was incorporated in 1980 and is headquartered in Fort Lauderdale, Florida.

financial_summary: AutoNation, Inc. is a mid-cap consumer cyclical business with a $6.0B market cap on $27.6B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +1% over the past three years and +3% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.

Returns on capital run at 22% against a 7% cost of capital — a 15-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat, and 17% gross margins are typical of commodity economics where competitors can replicate the product cheaply.
The company is burning through $198M of cash, and without positive owner earnings any valuation rests on hope rather than evidence.
On the balance sheet, debt is moderate at 3.1× net debt/EBITDA, serviceable in normal conditions but worth watching through a downturn, and interest coverage runs at 6.9×.

Management returns a meaningful 13.3% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.
